MBMM · 22nm Memristor-Based Main Memory2026-09 revision

Can 22nm ReRAM Replace
DDR5 in a Commodity DIMM?

Evaluation of 22nm Memristor-Based Main Memory (MBMM) in Commodity DIMM Architectures

Rebuilt on the corrected 2026-09 dataset: regenerated traces, one matched array organization, a published-silicon counterweight and a measured write distribution.

Yuval Kogan · Advisor: Prof. Shahar Kvatinsky · September 2026
01
Section 01

Motivation

Why system-level ReRAM, why now

Motivation1 / 4

The Memory Supply-Demand Crisis

  • Late 2025: DRAM wafer capacity reallocated to HBM for AI accelerators
  • Commodity main memory supply is getting squeezed by that shift
  • The question this creates: what else can serve as a DRAM alternative in standard DIMMs?
SayDRAM capacity is being pulled toward AI/HBM; commodity main memory is getting squeezed. That's the market pressure motivating alternatives.
Motivation2 / 4

Why ReRAM as a Candidate

  • Non-volatile - zero refresh power, by construction. DDR5 spends 6.5 to 9.1% of its module power on refresh it can never shed
  • Density potential - resistive cells can beat a scaling-limited DRAM capacitor
  • Logic-compatible process - fabricable on mature, high-volume CMOS nodes
  • The classic objection: endurance. Flagged now, and it is this revision's binding constraint.
SayThe pitch is refresh elimination and density. Endurance is the classic objection, flag it now so it doesn't feel dodged later - and this time the talk answers it with a measured write distribution rather than an assumption. Refresh share: Section 3.1.2, Table 3.
Motivation3 / 4

Device-level ReRAM is well studied.

System-level, commodity-DIMM behavior under real workloads is not.

SayMost ReRAM literature stops at the cell or macro. This project asks the system question - what happens when you put it in a DIMM behind a memory controller and run real traces through it.
Motivation4 / 4

What This Project Built

  • A cross-layer pipeline: NVSim (device physics) → NVMain 2.0 (system simulation)
  • Driven by traces regenerated for this revision - SPEC CPU2017 (502.gcc_r, 519.lbm_r) and STREAM through gem5, AI inference through SCALE-Sim
  • 20 memory configurations × 6 workloads, all at one matched array organization (2048 × 2048 subarrays, mux 64), so every cross-technology difference is a device difference
  • Three things added to the simulator for this revision: an end-to-end latency statistic, per-location wear counters, and a faithful Start-Gap wear-leveling decoder
SayThe matched organization is the single most important methodological change - the 3 September version characterized the two cells at different column-mux ratios, which confounded cell type with organization. Everything downstream of that moved.
02
Section 02

Background

The architectures and the yardsticks

Background1 / 4

1T1R vs 1S1R, at a Matched Organization

Per 1 Gb chip, 2048 × 2048, mux 641T1R1S1RWhat it means
Cell size20F²4F²Selector cell is smaller
Read latency10.12 ns4.70 nsThe selector is the faster reader
Write latency15.26 ns24.59 nsThe transistor is the more symmetric writer
Peripheral leakage108.384 mW108.384 mWIdentical to three decimals
Die area12.008 mm²3.540 mm²3.4×, the one surviving device advantage

NVSim assigns memristor cells no leakage at all: chip leakage is peripheral circuitry and follows mat count, not access-device type. Cell area is architecture-dependent, not fixed - a DRAM-process recessed-channel 1T1R has hit 6F² in a commercial part [33].

SayThis slide is the correction. Earlier versions of this book reported a large leakage gap between these two cells and called it the deciding architectural fact. It was not a device effect at all: the two cells had been characterized at different column-mux ratios, so one had 256 mats and the other 2. Force the same organization and they leak the same. Book Table 1; the retirement is tabulated in Appendix D.
Background2 / 4

SLC vs MLC

  • SLC - 1 bit/cell, single resistance threshold. Full DIMM: 8 GiB
  • MLC - 2 bits/cell via Iterative Step-and-Verify (ISPV) programming. Same 64 chips, 16 GiB
  • NVSim crashes simulating MLC's iterative sensing natively, so this project derives an analytical penalty method from the same EMBER macro's two publications (Upton et al., ESSCIRC 2023 [6]; Levy et al., IEEE JSSC 2024 [31]): 1.5× read latency, 3.263× write latency, 1.1× read energy, 3.0× write energy
  • Because leakage is per chip and MLC puts twice the capacity behind the same chips, MLC halves the per-gigabyte power penalty
  • The MLC latency figures in this deck are lower bounds: this project's generator books the cell write pulse as bank-recovery time, off the request path, so "MLC is barely slower" is a consequence of that mapping, not a device finding
SayThe multipliers are stated because they are this project's own derivation, not a citation - and they were re-sourced twice during the fidelity audit (items 13 and 14). Book Table 1 note.
Background3 / 4

The Cast of Characters

ConfigurationModuleRole in this study
DDR5-4800 (two 32-bit subchannels, BL16)16 GiBCommodity baseline - the real target to beat
PCM (legacy, 2009 lineage)4 GiBHistorical NVM reference; inherited constants, not NVSim-characterized
1T1R SLC / MLC8 / 16 GiBTransistor-gated ReRAM, NVSim-projected timings
1S1R SLC / MLC8 / 16 GiBSelector-gated ReRAM, NVSim-projected timings
1T1R SILICON / 1S1R SILICON8 GiBThe counterweight: same module, published fabricated-chip timings

Every technology is judged on latency, density and endurance, with power as a closely related fourth. All access at 64 bytes; two channels; identical 250 ms trace window.

The two SILICON rows use Micron/Sony's 27nm 16 Gb 1T1R (2.3 us read / 11.7 us write) [49] and SanDisk/Toshiba's 24nm 32 Gb 1S1R cross-point (40 us / 230 us) [48]. PCM's baseline is a black-box timing/energy model with no stated access device; the shipped product it evokes, Intel Optane, is a 1S1R cross-point [42], not modeled here.

SayName the SILICON rows out loud here, because they appear beside every latency number for the rest of the talk. They are the honest ceiling on the projection.
Background4 / 4

Where This Sits

  • Device-level ReRAM literature: extensive
  • System-level, DIMM-scale, workload-driven evaluation: the gap this fills
  • One real-hardware anchor point exists: Intel Optane DC PMM, the only NVM main-memory module ever shipped, measured 305 ns idle random-read latency against 81 ns for DRAM [32] - a different device architecture, so never benchmarked against directly, but the field's one genuine real-silicon data point
SayHonest positioning. Optane is real, measured, third-party data - worth naming even though it is architecturally different (selector-gated PCM) and cannot be a number-for-number comparison. Book Section 1.3.

Orchestrated end-to-end by mbmm_master.py - "The Gate-Keeper" (Section 2.2)

New gates in this revision: NVSim must print the forced 2048 Rows x 2048 Columns or the run fails; the generator refuses a timing split that does not sum to the device latency; every trace carries a provenance sidecar.

SayNVSim only ever characterizes ONE chip - that is what crosses the boundary at step 1 to 2. Everything from step 3 onward is NVMain replicating that single chip a small, fixed number of times and wrapping it in its own controller. This bridge is itself a contribution, and this revision added gates to it so the two silent failures it hid cannot recur.
Methodology2 / 9

One Chip → a Full DIMM

1 Gb
per-chip capacity (gigabit, not gigabyte; Table 1)
1–64
chips replicated per config - single → 8chip → 16chip → full DIMM
800 MHz
ReRAM DIMM interface: a disclosed assumption, no ReRAM citation (PCM 400, DDR5 2400 MHz)
8 / 16 GiB
full-DIMM capacity, SLC / MLC - now matching the physical module exactly
2
channels, matched to DDR5's two subchannels (16-chip and full DIMM only)

64 × 1 Gb ÷ 8 = 8 GiB SLC; MLC's 2 bits/cell doubles it to 16 GiB. The simulated capacity now matches the physical module exactly. It did not before, and that was not harmless: it changed which rank an address decoded to, which is the mechanism behind the whole scaling result (see: Since the 3 September review).

SayThe capacity fix is the quiet one that moved Section 3.2. Channels are formed by splitting ranks, so a one-rank module (single chip, 8 chips) stays single-channel - that detail matters on the channel-control slide later. Book Section 2.3; Appendix D, "Simulated module capacity".
Methodology3 / 9

The Bridge, in Parameters

NVSim output (Table 1) [3]

  • Read / write latency (ns)
  • Read / write energy (nJ)
  • Leakage (mW/chip)
  • Die area (mm²), subarray geometry

NVMain input (Sections 2.1, 3.1.6) [4]

  • tRCD + tCAS (cycles)
  • Erd / Ewr (nJ, per access)
  • Eactstdby / Eprestdby (nJ, per cycle)
  • ROWS / COLS / RANKS / BANKS

The largest single correction of this revision lives in this box. The generator wrote the full NVSim device read latency into both tRCD and tCAS, charging every read the device twice. It now splits: for 1T1R SLC, tRCD 4 + tCAS 5 at 800 MHz = 11.25 ns against a 10.12 ns device read, and validation refuses any configuration where the two do not sum.

SayThis is what "the bridge" does at the field level - unit and granularity conversion, not new physics. The read double-count is why the ReRAM latencies in this deck are roughly a third of the ones the 3 September version reported. Book Section 3.1.1; revision plan decision 37.
Methodology4 / 9

Real Workloads, Regenerated From Scratch

TraceCompleted in the 250 ms windowWhole traceSpanWhat it isolates
GCC (502.gcc_r)519,568545,566sustainedCompute-bound: static leakage, DIMM mostly idle
LBM (519.lbm_r)5,564,70410,779,425sustainedSustained streaming: dynamic energy, endurance worst case
STREAM (real benchmark)5,994,37848,439,056sustainedBandwidth baseline, two reads per write
AlexNet IFMAP (Conv2)1,269,5991,269,60060.5 usRead storm: controller queueing
AlexNet OFMAP (Conv2)135,423135,4244.5 usWrite storm: the write penalty
GPT-2 IFMAP65,53565,5362.2 usMax-parallelism AI read

gem5 O3 runs with L1 and L2 caches, 500 M instructions fast-forwarded, 400 M (gcc) or 300 M (lbm, STREAM) detailed, first 10 ms discarded as warm-up, then a 250 ms matched window. Each trace reconciles exactly with gem5's own memory-controller request counters. The three gem5 traces run longer than the window, so only part of each is replayed. The three AI bursts end inside it, so their two counts differ only by the single request still in flight when the window closes.

A seventh workload, 505.mcf_r, is absent: gem5 panics inside the benchmark's own input reader 0.13 ms into the detailed region, identically on two attempts. That is a benchmark-binary fault, not a pipeline fault.

SayThree things here are corrections, not just description. The old traces were captured with a parser whose line-matching rule kept about four records per real request; the old window sat inside each benchmark's start-up burst; and the SCALE-Sim parser kept one address per row instead of every address, undercounting the AI traces by up to tenfold. All three are in Appendix D. Also: "AlexNet Layer 1" is SCALE-Sim's zero-indexed layer1 folder, which is AlexNet's SECOND convolution layer - in this and every earlier version.
Methodology5 / 9

Baselines

  • DDR5-4800 - two independent 32-bit subchannels of 32 banks, 8 devices, 16 GiB, 64 B delivered as a 16-beat burst. Every device timing is taken from JEDEC JESD79-5 [10] with three documented exceptions: where NVMain keeps one rank-wide value and JEDEC splits it short/long by bank group (tCCD, tWTR, tRRD) the short value is used, which favors DDR5. A handful of NVMain-specific keys with no DDR5 counterpart keep template values. The earlier claim that this baseline was modelled to the letter of JESD79-5 is withdrawn: it is JEDEC-sourced with stated judgements, and the values were transcribed from a public mirror rather than an official copy of the standard
  • A 64 B cross-check run separates granularity from module shape: nearly equal on the CPU traces (79.6 against 83.1 ns under GCC), but 3.4× faster in the controller on the dense AI write burst. It is a legacy-shape reference, not a JEDEC DDR5 configuration - its tCCD of 4 cycles sits below the JEDEC floor of 8, kept so the 64-bit 8-beat channel shape survives - so its advantage is optimistic and the two-subchannel primary stays conservative
  • Legacy PCM (2009) [11] - architectural framing only; its timing and energy constants trace to Choi et al. ISSCC 2012 [41] and were never run through this project's NVSim pipeline
SayDDR5 is the real target to beat. One thing to know cold: the DDR5 baseline here is deliberately the honest, conservative one - it pays JEDEC bus serialization and it gets its power-down credit, both of which work against ReRAM in the comparisons that follow.
Methodology6 / 9

Two Latency Numbers, Defined Once

Total
Queue entry to completion. The like-for-like device comparison. Cannot see time a request spends waiting to be accepted at all
End to end
Trace timestamp to completion. Added to NVMain for this revision. The saturation measure

Where a configuration keeps up, the two agree to a fraction of a memory cycle: under GCC, 1T1R SLC posts 41.4 ns total against 40.9 ns end to end.

Where it does not, they diverge by orders of magnitude: the legacy PCM baseline posts 5,136.8 ns total against 62.2 ms end to end under LBM.

A configuration whose two latencies have separated is not slow. It is failing to keep up.

SayThis slide exists because the classic statistic is not safe on a saturated run, and two of the results later in the talk only make sense once both definitions are on the table. Book Section 3.1.1.
Methodology7 / 9

I Audited My Own Toolchain

14

silent failure modes found in the standard NVSim → NVMain flow - 13 repaired and validated, each against a device-level anchor or exact predicted arithmetic

  • Leakage and access energy were silently ignored by the power model - wired in and re-run
  • DDR5's refresh timing and supply parameters were inherited unrescaled from a DDR3-1333 template - corrected to real DDR5-4800 JEDEC values
  • Trace provenance was weaker than the methodology claimed - every trace regenerated from scratch with a sidecar, each reconciling exactly with gem5's own counters
  • ReRAM's MLC multipliers were unsourced - re-sourced to [6] / [31] and re-derived twice
  • Idle power-down was disabled in NVMain's source - restored for every technology; DDR5 now realizes real savings, while ReRAM's power-down energy is a disclosed no-savings placeholder
SayPresent this as rigor, not confession. One item is not repaired at all and cannot be: item 6's GPT-2 generator configuration was never preserved. Item 8 counts among the thirteen repaired, with the disclosed caveat that DDR5's IDD currents are vendor specification limits, because no vendor publishes a typical DDR5 IDD figure to use instead. Full list is in the backup.
Methodology8 / 9

What "Validated" Means Here

Limitation, stated up front
  • Validation = internal consistency - NVMain reproduces NVSim's own numbers to 0.0% error, and every repair is checked against a device-level anchor or exact predicted arithmetic
  • NOT validation against a real fabricated chip or a measured DDR5 DIMM
  • Which is exactly why the two published-silicon configurations run on every trace, and why they sit beside every latency table in the book
SayBe the one who raises this before someone in the audience does. Book Section 2.2.
Methodology9 / 9

Assumptions That Shape Every Result Next

  • Every ReRAM latency rests on NVSim's array-core projection, which no fabricated part has matched - the SILICON rows are the counterweight
  • Every endurance figure is a projection from a write distribution measured per location, never a measured lifetime
  • ReRAM power = no gating benefit claimed. Power-down runs in simulation, but its energy is an explicit no-savings placeholder, so every power ratio here is an upper bound
  • DDR5 power = datasheet specification-limit IDD currents; vendors publish no typical figure
  • Both module power figures count memory devices only: no register clock driver, power-management IC, PHY, termination or ReRAM-side controller, on either side
  • MLC latency is a lower bound: the cell write pulse sits off the request path in this project's generator
  • The GPT-2 trace's original SCALE-Sim configuration was never preserved, so it stands as a representative parallel-read pattern, not a validated GPT-2 capture. All three AI traces are microsecond bursts, not sustained workloads
SayRead every number in the next 25 minutes through this lens. Two of these bound a headline rather than qualifying it: without a fabricated part at NVSim's timings there is no latency advantage, and without wear leveling substantially better than single-region Start-Gap there is no ten-year lifetime. Book Conclusion.
04
Section 04

Results

Latency, power, scaling, endurance

Results · Latency1 / 7

Compute-Bound: ReRAM Is Faster

  • 1S1R SLC 36.8 ns, 1T1R SLC 41.4 ns against DDR5's 83.1 ns
  • A DDR5 row miss pays tRCD plus CAS, 16.25 + 16.67 ns, then senses and restores a capacitor
  • A 2048 × 2048 ReRAM subarray reads in 10.12 ns and has no row to precharge
  • But only 11.25 ns of that 41.4 is NVSim device time (tRCD + tCAS). The other 30.2 ns is NVMain's protocol cycle counts at the assumed 800 MHz interface

At NVSim-projected device timings only. With published silicon timings the same DIMM is 11.9 us and 379 us under GCC and does not complete the LBM window; on the write-dominated AI burst ReRAM is slower than DDR5. Roughly three quarters of the ReRAM figure is an interface assumption, not a device measurement: the direction is robust (ReRAM stays below DDR5 at all three clocks measured, and below the corrected, slower DDR5), the magnitude is model-dependent.

SayThis is the reversal, and it is arithmetic rather than a surprise. Give the decomposition out loud: 11.25 ns of device, 30.2 ns of protocol at a clock this book assumes and cannot cite. Read 41.4 against 83.1 as the outcome of one clock choice, not as a device ratio. The 3 September version had ReRAM comfortably slower than DDR5 here; the retired figures are on the change-log slides. Three corrections compound to get to this one: the read double-count, the trace regeneration, and the matched organization. Book Table 2.
Results · Latency2 / 7

And Nothing Fabricated Comes Close

The identical trace through the identical module geometry at published fabricated-chip timings: 11.9 us (Micron/Sony 16 Gb 1T1R [49]) and 379 us (SanDisk/Toshiba 32 Gb 1S1R [48]) under GCC. Neither completes the LBM window.

The honest statement: a 22nm ReRAM array core, if it can be built at NVSim's projected timings, beats DDR5 on compute-bound traffic, and nothing yet built comes close. The gap between those two sentences is the engineering problem, and it is far larger than any difference between 1T1R and 1S1R.

At NVSim-projected device timings only. With published silicon timings the same DIMM is 11.9 us and 379 us under GCC and does not complete the LBM window; on the write-dominated AI burst ReRAM is slower than DDR5.

SayDo not let the previous slide travel without this one. This is the single most important addition of the revision on the latency axis. Book Table 2 and its note.
Results · Latency3 / 7

Sustained Streaming: No Longer a Deficit Regime

Every ReRAM track completes the entire 250 ms window - 5,564,704 of 5,564,704 requests - exactly as DDR5 does, at 9.54 M writes/s sustained. 1T1R SLC averages 43.1 ns and 1S1R SLC 38.1 ns against DDR5's 78.3 ns; under STREAM, 42.3 and 37.3 against 79.4 ns. The old trace offered roughly four times LBM's real request rate, from inside its start-up burst.

What LBM still exposes is where the resistive technologies fail: PCM completes 50.2%, and the two silicon configurations 18.2% and 1.0%. Their end-to-end latencies (62.2 ms, 102.3 ms, 123.6 ms) show the backlog, not the device.

At NVSim-projected device timings only (published silicon: 11.9 us and 379 us, LBM window not completed); and ReRAM is slower than DDR5 on the write-dominated AI burst.

SayThe 3 September version reported ReRAM completing only a fraction of this window and read it as a device-speed ordering; the change-log slide gives the figures. It was an artifact of a fourfold-duplicated trace. Say that plainly - it is the change most likely to be remembered from the last review. Book Section 3.1.1; Appendix D, "LBM completion".
Results · Latency4 / 7

AI Read Burst: a Queueing Measurement

The AI-inference deficit this book previously reported is gone (see: Since the 3 September review), and both its causes are understood: the read double-count inflated every ReRAM latency, and the old AI traces undercounted addresses tenfold, which changed the shape of the offered burst.

1T1R SLC 143.3 ns and 1S1R SLC 130.1 ns against DDR5's 222.1 ns; end to end, 106.3 and 97.9 us against 139.1 us. But every one of these configurations spends three orders of magnitude more time waiting for admission than being served. No conclusion about sustained AI-inference serving can be drawn from a 2.2 microsecond single-layer capture.

At NVSim-projected device timings only (published silicon: 11.9 us and 379 us, LBM window not completed); and ReRAM is slower than DDR5 on the write-dominated AI burst.

SayResist the temptation to sell this as a win. The ordering is real and it favors ReRAM because a higher per-request service rate drains the burst sooner - but the measurement is about the queue. A representative full-model trace is future work. Book Section 3.1.1.
Results · Latency5 / 7

The Write Burst: the One Regime ReRAM Loses

Under the write-dominated AlexNet OFMAP burst the ordering inverts: DDR5 averages 234.3 ns while 1T1R SLC pays 353.1, 1S1R SLC 391.5, 1T1R MLC 512.0 and 1S1R MLC 652.9 ns. ReRAM loses this regime by a clear but moderate margin: DDR5 is 1.51× faster than 1T1R SLC and 1.67× than 1S1R SLC, rising to 2.19× and 2.79× against the two MLC tracks.

Two bounds point opposite ways. The ReRAM side is a lower bound on the deficit, because the cell write pulse is off the request path in this model; the DDR5 side now carries JEDEC write recovery and write latency rather than DDR3-template cycle counts, which is why the deficit is smaller than this book quoted before that correction.

1T1R SLC is the most write-tolerant ReRAM configuration in the suite (2.5× degradation against DDR5's 1.10×) even though it is not the fastest reader: the access transistor makes the device symmetric, 15.26 against 10.12 ns, while a 1S1R write costs 5.2× its own read. This ordering is what confines MLC to read-dominant roles.

SayNote what changed about the MLC story. Under LBM and GCC the MLC tracks are not slower than their SLC siblings at all, because NVMain books write recovery as bank-busy time rather than request latency and the banks have idle time to absorb it. The penalty only surfaces where the offered write rate keeps the banks busy - which is exactly here. Book Section 3.1.1.
Results · Latency6 / 7

Why End-to-End Is the Right Metric

A deeper queue raises the classic latency metric and lowers the time the workload actually waits, because a short queue reports a fast average over the few requests it admits while the rest of the burst backs up outside the controller.

The metric that improves with a shallower queue is the metric that is measuring the wrong thing. On GCC and LBM the depth makes no difference at all, at 8, 32 or 128 alike, because the queue never fills.

SayThis is the one experiment that separates the two definitions cleanly, and it is the argument for reporting end-to-end latency. Two scoping notes if asked: the depth flag reaches the ReRAM configurations only, and every configuration completes the identical request population at every depth. Book Section 3.1.1; Appendix A, "Memory Controller Queue Depth".
Results · Latency7 / 7

The Interface Clock Is a Real Lever

Measured rather than asserted: media, traces and window unchanged, baselines left at their own clocks, every configuration completing the identical request population. Worth 2.2× on the CPU traces, taking 1T1R SLC from 41.4 to 19.0 ns against a DDR5 baseline of 83.1.

It is not the binding term in the dense-burst regime: tripling the clock buys 1.8× in the controller and 1.7× end to end, because the queue is what the burst is waiting on. And it costs nothing in power - interface clock does not enter the NVSim leakage figure at all.

At NVSim-projected device timings only (published silicon: 11.9 us and 379 us, LBM window not completed); and ReRAM is slower than DDR5 on the write-dominated AI burst.

Say800 MHz is a disclosed modeling assumption with no independent ReRAM-interface citation. It is positioned between two precedents: twice NVMain's PCM reference basis, and below the DDR4-2666 electricals that carried DDR-T on shipped Optane DIMMs. The only real ReRAM chip I/O clocks located, Fujitsu SPI parts at 5 to 10 MHz, run far slower. Book Section 2.3.
Results · Power1 / 4

The Leakage Gap Was an Organization Artifact

Force both cells to the same 2048 × 2048 subarray at mux 64 and NVSim gives them identical peripheral leakage, 108.384 mW per 1 Gb chip. The gap earlier versions of this book called the deciding architectural fact of the evaluation does not exist as a device effect.

The mechanism is visible in the sensitivity: at 1024 × 1024 there are four times the mats, each with half the sense amplifiers, so leakage roughly doubles - for both cells alike. The conclusion does not depend on which organization is matched.

SayOwn this one. The two cells had been characterized at hand-set, unequal column muxes, never stated in the book, so every device-level comparison confounded cell type with organization. What survives is die area, 3.4 times in the selector's favor. Book Section 3.1.2; Appendix D, "Per-chip leakage".
Results · Power2 / 4

Power per Gigabyte: the Central Negative Result

The full ReRAM DIMM draws 6.94 W for 8 GiB, 99.96% of it static, against 0.797 W for a 16 GiB DDR5 module under GCC: 12.7× to 17.4× DDR5 per gigabyte for the SLC tracks, 6.4× to 8.7× as MLC.

Both module figures count memory devices only. No register clock driver, power-management IC, PHY, termination or ReRAM-side controller, on either side. A real DDR5 RDIMM draws watts rather than 0.797 W, and a fixed per-module overhead added to both sides would compress this ratio - but it moves the gating break-even of the next slide the other way, and those two statements must be kept apart.

The ratio is also an upper bound: DDR5 carries its JEDEC power-down credit while ReRAM's power-down energy is an explicit no-savings placeholder, so the model cannot price a ReRAM module that gates its periphery.

SayThis is still the central negative result and it should be said without softening - but the gap is a third of what this deck showed yesterday, because DDR5's own static power was undercounted fourfold by an upstream NVMain accounting defect and its write path was still DDR3-template. Both are corrected; every ReRAM number is unchanged. Attacking the leakage floor is a circuit problem in the sense amplifiers and decoders, not a choice between access devices. Book Section 3.1.2, Table 3; Appendix A.
Results · Power3 / 4

What Would Close It, and What the Selector Costs

94.3%
of the static component gated to break even with DDR5 per GiB at 22nm (80.8% at a 12nm-class port)
94–98%
idleness, from the 2 to 6% memory-bandwidth utilization reported for web-serving deployments [21]. The threshold now sits inside that band, not above it

The band brackets break-even. At its idle end (98% gated) the module would draw 0.142 W against DDR5's 0.399 W for the same 8 GiB, a ratio of 0.36× - below DDR5. At the busy end (94%) it would draw 0.419 W, 1.05× above.

So the arithmetic does not forbid parity for that deployment class, and on the optimistic reading it implies it. What this project cannot do is price a gated module at all, because no measured ReRAM power-down energy exists. Neither the parity nor its impossibility is demonstrated here.

And the device-only scope cuts against the bracketed parity, not for it: the same overhead is carried by 8 GiB of ReRAM against 16 GiB of DDR5, so the required gating fraction rises with it - 94.3% at zero, 97.9% at 0.5 W per module, and beyond 0.79 W no gating fraction reaches parity at all.

0 mW
the analytic selector layer adds to standby power: unbiased crossbar lines have no voltage across their cells
7.56 / 0.076
mW per chip during an access, at an ovonic-threshold-switch bound and at a best-published FAST-selector bound [9]
1666
cells a side: the OTS bound's tile ceiling. It cannot keep a 2048-cell tile valid

NVSim models no selector physics at all, so this is a standalone analytic layer on top of it, using the crossbar read model of [51]. 1S1R at this organization is conditional on selector quality - which is a real caveat on the density case, not a footnote.

SayThis is a change of tone, not just of value: with DDR5's power corrected, gating is no longer arithmetically out of reach. Say all three parts or none - the threshold is inside the cited band, the band brackets break-even, and the model still cannot price a gated module. If asked whether that makes ReRAM competitive on power: no, because the same per-module overhead that flatters the ungated ratio pushes the gating threshold up, and past about 0.79 W of overhead nothing reaches parity. Book Sections 3.1.2 and 3.3 read as a pair; results/selector_layer.json.
Results · Power4 / 4

Efficiency: the Four Tracks Converge

  • At module level the four ReRAM tracks fall within 1.2× of one another and 4.4× to 5.3× behind DDR5
  • The large intra-ReRAM efficiency gap this book previously reported was the leakage artifact propagated into the power term (see: Since the 3 September review)
  • Per gigabyte, which is the form the chart plots: 9.4 / 8.7 / 5.3 / 4.7× DDR5, so the four tracks span 2.0× there
  • Legacy PCM lands at 1.3× DDR5 at module level and beats it on two traces, but sits at 5.1× per gigabyte, behind MLC ReRAM
SayPCM now beats the corrected DDR5 on module PDP for two traces, and it is still not a headline - the book gives three reasons and none is small. Its latency averages on LBM and STREAM cover only the 50.2% and 46.1% it completed, so two of its six geometric-mean terms are lower bounds. Its module is 4 GiB, and per gigabyte the ordering reverses: 5.1x against 4.7x for 1S1R MLC. And its static floor is a constant inherited from NVMain's bundled example configuration, not a characterized device. The defensible statement is narrow: nothing in this ReRAM matrix improves on a legacy PCM configuration at module level, while MLC ReRAM does improve on it per gigabyte. Book Section 3.1.3, Table 4 and its note.
Results · Scaling1 / 2

Chip Count Buys Capacity and Pays Leakage

  • Static power is exactly 1, 8, 16 and 64 times 108.384 mW, to six digits, identical for all four tracks
  • The three CPU traces improve 6.4% to 10.4% across the physically realizable points, with no monotonic trend
  • Delivered bandwidth is identical at all four architectures: these traces are offered-rate limited, not device limited
  • Rank depth is worth at most 7.5%, and only on the three CPU traces; on the three AI traces it buys exactly nothing
SayThe trajectories run almost vertically: power climbs an order of magnitude while latency moves a few percent. The two-leakage-tier picture the 3 September version plotted, one family scaling into infeasibility and the other holding a commodity envelope, is withdrawn - both families sit on the same static floor. Book Section 3.2, Table 8.
Results · Scaling2 / 2

It Is the Channel, Not the Rank

The two AI read bursts gain 1.68× between 8 and 16 chips - but that step doubles chips and channels together. Hold the channel count at one and the three points collapse onto each other. Restore the second channel and the queue term halves while the device term does not move at all, 29.0 against 29.1 ns.

Rank depth cannot help these traces because their footprints never leave one rank: GPT-2 IFMAP touches 1,024 distinct lines spanning 64.0 KiB and AlexNet IFMAP 1,094 lines spanning 68.4 KiB, both inside a single 128 KiB two-channel rank span. The simulator's own rank counters confirm it: ranks 1 to 3 see zero reads and zero writes.

SayThis is the corrected form of the "flatline" argument that has been running since 3 September, and the correction is that it is a flatline in rank depth rather than in chip count. Among the module-organization choices this matrix varies, channel count is the one that moves burst latency - and only for queue-bound traffic. Book Section 3.2.
Results · Viability1 / 5

Density: the Selector's Real Advantage

  • 1S1R SLC 1.24× DDR5, MLC 2.47×
  • 1T1R 0.36× and 0.73× - the 20F² cell cost
  • Every ratio is linear in the assumed cell area: a 14nm embedded macro at 112F² would drag 1T1R to about 0.07×, a 6F² recessed-channel part would lift it to about 1.2×
SayThese numbers moved a lot, in both directions, because die area is organization-dependent in exactly the same way leakage is; the change-log slide gives the old pair. The sensitivity to the assumed cell area is worth stating out loud - it is the largest uncertainty in the density case. Book Section 3.3, Tables 6 and 7.
Results · Viability2 / 5

Node Scaling: Where This Could Go

Bounding claims, not measurements: the 16nm and 12nm columns are geometry rather than NVSim characterizations, they optimistically assume peripheral circuits shrink with the cell array, and selector device physics below the 2x-nm regime is unvalidated. 1T1R cannot deck-stack at all - its access transistor is a front-end-of-line device.

SaySay "projection" out loud. The badge is on the chart for a reason. Book Table 6.
Results · Viability3 / 5

Endurance: the Leveling Decides It

At 64 GiB and a best-sourced 106 cycle rating [47], ideal uniform leveling gives 38.6 years under GCC and 3.6 under LBM, while no leveling at all gives 7.7 and 23.2 hours. Four to five orders of magnitude, and the whole lifetime claim lives in the mechanism, not in the cell.

The traces are sparse: GCC touches 577 row locations, LBM 826 and STREAM 1,954, out of 1,048,576 at this capacity. A workload that concentrates its entire write stream on a few hundred locations exhausts them regardless of how much unused capacity sits beside them.

SayEvery number here is a PROJECTION from a write distribution measured per location in the simulator, never a measured lifetime - say the word. The previous version quoted only the ideal-leveling column, described it as a capacity law, and never measured the alternative. Book Section 3.1.4, Table 5.
Results · Viability4 / 5

Start-Gap Does Not Close That Gap

  • A faithful implementation of Qureshi et al.'s Start-Gap remapper [52] was added to the simulator: one gap line, all lines rotating by one every 100 writes
  • Over a single whole-module region it recovers essentially nothing: 7.7 hours under GCC against 7.7 without leveling, 23.2 under LBM against 23.2
  • The reason is structural, not a bug. Rotating the gap once through a 64 GiB module of 1.07 billion lines takes about 1011 writes, while the hottest line in these sparse footprints exhausts its 106-cycle budget after about 106. The hot line dies long before relief arrives
  • Qureshi's reported 97% of ideal was obtained against a very different write distribution, and it does not transfer to sparse footprints
  • It can get worse with capacity. The rotation period grows with the region while the gap still advances one line per hundred writes. Projected under randomized Start-Gap, LBM falls from 0.22 years at 8 GiB to 0.20 at 64 and 0.05 at 128
  • Randomizing the region assignment recovers part of the ideal: 0.20 years under LBM, 0.96 under STREAM, and still nothing under GCC, whose footprint is too small to randomize over
SayThis is the most counter-intuitive result in the revision and it is worth slowing down for. The mechanism is sound and the implementation is exact; the failure is a property of these workloads' write distributions. One disclosure: the decoder's own relocation traffic, about a 1% write overhead, is charged as wear in the projection but is not issued as traffic in the simulation, so no latency or power figure in this work carries the cost of running Start-Gap. Book Section 3.1.4.
Results · Viability5 / 5

Stated the Way a Designer Needs It

The same equation solved for endurance rather than for time: the per-cell cycle count a ten-year life at 64 GiB would demand.

WorkloadWrite rateRequired endurance, ideal levelingRequired endurance, randomized Start-Gap
GCC0.88 M/s2.6 × 1056.3 × 106
LBM9.54 M/s2.8 × 1066.5 × 106
STREAM7.99 M/s2.3 × 1064.3 × 106

Against a best-sourced production planning value of 106 [47], with 104 and 107 carried as bounds. So GCC clears it comfortably under ideal leveling; the two streaming workloads need 2.3 to 2.8× the rated cycle count under ideal leveling, and 4.3 to 6.5× under randomized Start-Gap.

The 107 SLC rating earlier versions of this book used was cited to a source that gives no SLC or MLC rating at all. That citation has been withdrawn.

SayThis table is in Shahar's own framing from the 3 September review, which asked for the requirement rather than the outcome. It is also the cleanest statement of what would have to be true for a ten-year module. Book Section 3.1.4, Table 5.

Section 05

Contributions

What this delivers

Contributions1 / 2

What This Delivers

  • An open-sourced NVSim → NVMain cross-layer pipeline for ReRAM DIMM evaluation, now with forced-organization gates, provenance sidecars on every trace, per-location wear counters and an end-to-end latency statistic
  • A 14-item toolchain fidelity audit, 13 repaired and each validated - reusable methodology beyond this project's own numbers
  • Three additions contributed back to NVMain 2.0: the end-to-end latency statistic, the per-location wear map, and a faithful Start-Gap decoder
  • An analytic selector layer supplying the sneak-path physics NVSim does not model at all
  • A corrected characterization: this revision withdraws three of the headline claims the 3 September version made, because the experiments that supported them were not controlled
SayThe last bullet is the one to lead with in a thesis defense. Withdrawing a headline because the experiment was not controlled is the contribution, not the embarrassment.
Contributions2 / 2

22nm ReRAM is a dense, non-volatile, leakage-expensive medium that is latency-competitive at projected device timings: a plausible capacity tier behind a DRAM front end, and not a drop-in DDR5 replacement.

At NVSim-projected device timings only. With published silicon timings the same DIMM is 11.9 us and 379 us under GCC and does not complete the LBM window; on the write-dominated AI burst ReRAM is slower than DDR5.

The choice between 1T1R and 1S1R decides die area (3.4×) and write symmetry (1.5× against 5.2× write-to-read at the device), and decides essentially nothing about power or system efficiency. Both are conditional: 1S1R on a selector better than today's production ovonic threshold switch, 1T1R on a cell area no fabricated logic-process part has reached.

On power the honest statement now has three parts and needs all three: the ungated gap is 12.7× to 17.4× per gigabyte, an upper bound, counting memory devices only; break-even gating at 94.3% sits inside the idleness band this book cites, so the arithmetic brackets parity for that deployment class; and the model cannot price a gated module, because no measured ReRAM power-down energy exists. Neither parity nor its impossibility is demonstrated here.

Making it a replacement still requires attacking the peripheral-leakage floor directly - a circuit problem in the sense amplifiers and decoders, not a choice between access devices.

SayThis is the narrower recommendation the corrected data supports, and it no longer turns on the access device at all. Book Conclusion.
06
Section 06

Future Work

What would change the verdict

Future Work1 / 2

The Two Things That Bound the Headlines

  • A wear-leveling scheme substantially better than single-region Start-Gap. Without it there is no ten-year lifetime at any capacity. Randomized region assignment already recovers part of the gap in projection; the next step is a scheme evaluated against these measured write distributions rather than against Qureshi's
  • A real ReRAM power-gating characterization. The mechanism is live in simulation, but no source splits ReRAM leakage into gatable and ungatable fractions, so its power-down energy is an honest zero-savings placeholder. This is a literature and analysis task, not new simulation infrastructure, and it is what stands between the stated 94.3% threshold and a gated number

Alongside them: a representative full-model AI trace. Every AI conclusion in this deck rests on microsecond single-layer captures whose footprints never leave one rank - the one case that would decide the scaling question is a trace with a large footprint and a sustained arrival rate above one controller's service rate, and none of the six provides it.

SayFrame these as the boundary of the claims rather than as a wish list - the book's conclusion does exactly that. Book Sections 4.1 and 4.2.
Future Work2 / 2

Beyond That, by Theme

  • Leakage - attack the peripheral floor in the sense amplifiers and decoders; it is 99.96% of module power
  • Selector quality: an OTS that keeps a 2048-cell tile valid, or an organization sized to the 1666-cell ceiling
  • Recessed-channel 1T1R density, which could overturn the density verdict on its own
  • Node scaling and 3D deck stacking, re-derived at scaled geometries rather than projected
  • Write path - a wide internal word behind a write-combining buffer; controller-level write buffering against the 2.5× to 5.0× write degradation
  • Start-Gap gap-move traffic issued as real requests, so its latency and power cost are priced
  • Model fidelity - native MLC logic: resolve NVSim's Mat.cpp floating-point exception, replacing the analytical penalty method
  • An Optane comparison row built from the shipped module's published behavior, as the field's one real anchor
  • PCM's zero power-down activity under its FRFCFS-WQF controller, not yet root-caused
  • Validation - any end-to-end check against measured hardware; today every result is internal to the toolchain

Thank You

Questions - and the backup slides are next if this runs long.

Backup3 / 5

Start-Gap On Versus Off, and Why No Before/After

  • The primary matrix runs with the Start-Gap decoder enabled; a full sensitivity run was done with it off
  • Wear statistics and latency are identical both ways on GCC, LBM and the AlexNet output map
  • That is the expected outcome, not a defect. With one whole-module region of 134,217,728 lines and one gap move per 100 writes, a 250 ms window completes about 10-5 of one rotation, and the gap starts at the top of the module while these workloads occupy low addresses
  • The simulator cannot show wear leveling at work inside any feasible window. Its effect is therefore carried by the projection, whose model was validated against a write-by-write simulator to within 0.3%
  • So this deck shows no before-and-after hot-spot figure, deliberately
  • One further disclosure: NVMain's RowModel books wear per row (1024 column lines), so the raw per-row maximum overstates per-cell wear by up to 1024×. It is used only for the on-versus-off comparison; per-line wear comes from the trace-level analysis
SayIf Shahar asks "did you show the leveling working", this is the answer: no, and here is precisely why it cannot be shown in a 250 ms window, and here is what carries the claim instead. Book Section 3.1.4; Appendix D, "Start-Gap on versus off".

What Shahar's Notes Uncovered

  • Note 6 (the leakage gap). Asking where the 47x came from led to the organization audit, and from there to the matched 2048 × 2048 rerun that retired it, to the corrected die areas and densities, and to the analytic selector layer that now supplies the physics NVSim never modeled
  • Note 8 (endurance). Asking for the requirement rather than the outcome led to per-location wear counters in NVMain, a faithful Start-Gap decoder, three leveling policies projected from a measured distribution instead of one assumed, and the required-endurance table in his own framing
  • Between them they also surfaced the read double-count, the 512 GB capacity artifact, the DDR5 module mismatch and the trace time base - none of which were in either note, but all of which were found by auditing what the notes questioned

Three headline claims are withdrawn in this revision. The book's Appendix D tabulates all 43 changed rows with the old value, the new value, the cause and the evidence path.
